responseText:
I can’t inspect your calendar, so I can’t tell you which specific events would be conflicted. Below is a concise, practical walkthrough of the typical knock‑on effects of moving a recurring “monthly board prep” from the first Tuesday to the second Tuesday, and what attendees will see. Use it to check your real calendar/recurring meetings.

What to think about / likely knock‑ons
- Relative timing to the board meeting
  - If the board meeting is later in the month (e.g., 3rd or 4th Tuesday): moving prep from the 1st to the 2nd Tuesday usually shortens the lead time for contributors (e.g., from two weeks to one week before the board). That affects deadlines, review cycles and time for revisions.
  - If the board meeting is on the 2nd Tuesday: moving prep to the 2nd will conflict or overlap with the actual board meeting.
  - If the board meeting is on the 1st Tuesday: moving prep to the 2nd moves prep after the meeting (likely undesirable).

- Common recurring events that often live on early-month Tuesdays
  - Finance month‑close reviews, executive team meetings, payroll/benefits reviews, audit/committee meetings, vendor calls or external advisor calls. Those may already sit on the 2nd Tuesday in some organizations.
  - All‑hands or departmental check‑ins that are scheduled “first/second Tuesday” patterns.

- Deadlines, deliverables, and workflows
  - Pack production schedule: authors, approvers and designers may need to accelerate deliverable deadlines (e.g., slide deck, financials, legal sign‑offs).
  - Review cycles (CFO/CEO review, legal review) may be compressed — expect more last‑minute updates.
  - External contributors (auditors, board members external to org) may need earlier notice for travel/availability.

- People/availability impacts
  - Some attendees who are free on the first Tuesday may be double‑booked on the second (regular standing meetings). Expect new conflicts for a subset of attendees.
  - Time‑zone effects: if you span time zones, shifting a week may place it near different local holidays or out‑of-office patterns.

What attendees will see (calendar behavior)
- If you reschedule the recurring series to the 2nd Tuesday:
  - Attendees receive a calendar update/reschedule notification for the series. Their calendars will reflect the series move (Outlook/Gmail update behavior varies slightly).
  - If the attendee has a recurring event at the new time, their calendar will show a conflict/overlap or they’ll see two items at the same time.
  - Reminders and reminders settings remain unless you change them; attendees may need to accept the updated invite if their client requires it.

- If you create a new event on the 2nd Tuesday instead of editing the series:
  - Attendees may see both the original (first Tuesday) and the new (second Tuesday) events until you cancel the old one — potential confusion and double‑booked invites.

- If you change only one occurrence:
  - Only that month’s occurrence will move; future months remain unchanged. Attendees see an exception on their calendar.

- Notifications & agenda/materials
  - They’ll get an update email/message about the date change if you send one; the meeting description, agenda, or attachments can be updated with the calendar change.
  - If you move the meeting closer to deliverables, attendees will receive revised deadlines or “board pack due” dates separately (and may see increased last‑minute email activity).

Practical checklist to run before you change anything
1. Identify the board meeting date relative to prep and the desired objective (do you want prep closer or further from the meeting?).  
2. Search shared calendars for recurring events on second Tuesdays (check all key attendees’ calendars).  
3. Check critical deadlines (financial close, packet publication, approvals) and recalc new deadlines with the new prep date.  
4. Poll or propose the change to key stakeholders (CEO, CFO, Governance Chair) before mass reschedule.  
5. Decide whether to reschedule the series (preferred) or create a new event and cancel the old series; plan communication accordingly.  
6. Communicate the change in one clear message explaining timeline shifts and any new deliverable deadlines.  
7. Allow a window for attendees to flag conflicts, then finalize.

Recommended communications
- Send a short advance note (2–4 weeks) explaining:
  - What you’re proposing (first → second Tuesday),
  - Why (brief rationale),
  - Immediate knock‑ons (new packet deadlines, potential conflicts),
  - Request people to flag conflicts within X days or use a scheduling poll.

If you want, I can:
- Draft the short notice/email to send to attendees (I can do that now), or
- Give a brief timeline template to recalc deliverables based on how many days earlier/later prep would be.

Which of those would help you next?
